title: Cover the Aggregate to Skip the Full Scan
description: A month-end aggregate scans the whole table to find recent rows; a covering index on the date range seeks straight to them. Why it matters: recent-data aggregates (dashboards, monthly summaries) are everywhere, and this is exactly why they slow down as history grows if nobody revisits the indexing.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

This lesson brings together two ideas from earlier in this course — range-based filtering with a leading key column, and covering indexes that eliminate extra lookups — into a very common analytical/reporting shape: a month-end aggregate report, summarizing totals over a recent date range, that currently scans an entire large table just to look at a small, recent slice of it.

The scenario: `SELECT Method, SUM(Amount) ... WHERE PaidAt >= '2025-12-01' GROUP BY Method` — a report totaling payments by method for the month of December. December represents only about 1/12th of the table's data (roughly 8%), yet the query reads all 400,000 rows every single time it runs, because there's no index on `PaidAt` at all — nothing tells SQL Server where in physical storage December's rows are, so the only option is to check every row and see if its date falls in range.

The fix draws on the same principle covered in the composite equality-plus-range lesson, but here it's even simpler because there's only one filtering condition, not two: build an index on `PaidAt` itself, so the table's rows become sorted by date. Once that index exists, SQL Server can seek directly to December 1st — jumping straight to the right starting point in the sorted structure, the same way you'd flip directly to a specific date's entry in a chronologically-organized filing system — and then simply read forward from there, since everything from that point onward (up to wherever December ends) is exactly the rows the report needs, sitting together, contiguously, in sorted order. No need to touch the other roughly 11/12ths of the table representing all the other months.

But this lesson pushes one step further than "just add an index on the filtered column," and that extra step is worth understanding well: the query doesn't just filter by date — it also needs `Method` and `Amount` to compute the actual aggregate (grouping by payment method, summing the amount for each group). If the index on `PaidAt` doesn't also carry `Method` and `Amount` along with it, SQL Server would still need a Key Lookup back to the full table for every one of the matching December rows, to go fetch those two additional columns — exactly the same "seek is fast, but there's an expensive lookup tacked onto every row" pattern covered in the covering-index lessons earlier in this course. So the fully effective fix here combines *both* ideas at once: build the index on `PaidAt` (so the range filter can seek), and also `INCLUDE (Method, Amount)` on that same index (so no lookup is needed once the matching rows are found) — `CREATE INDEX IX_Payments_PaidAt ON Payments(PaidAt) INCLUDE (Method, Amount)`. With both pieces in place, SQL Server can seek straight to December 1st in the index, read forward through exactly the qualifying rows, and compute the `SUM`/`GROUP BY` using only the data already present in the index — no trips back to the full table at all, no matter how big the table's other 11 months of history eventually grow.

This lesson is worth treating as a capstone example, precisely because it doesn't introduce a brand-new isolated concept — it shows how two techniques you've already learned separately (seeking a range via a sorted index, and covering a query so no lookups are needed) combine naturally in a single, very ordinary-looking report. Real production queries are frequently like this: not a single, pure textbook example of one specific problem, but a blend of two or three of these patterns stacked on top of each other, and being able to recognize each piece separately — "this needs a seekable range on the filter column" plus "this needs to also carry the other selected/aggregated columns so there's no lookup" — is exactly the skill that lets you diagnose and fix real, messier queries confidently.

Why does this matter in practice? Recent-data aggregates — month-end summaries, weekly rollups, "activity in the last 30 days" dashboards — are an extremely common category of report in almost every business system, and they share this exact structural shape: a growing table where the report only ever cares about a small, recent slice of it. Without the right index, this kind of report gets slower and slower over time as the *entire* table grows, even though the actual amount of relevant, recent data being summarized stays roughly constant — which is exactly the kind of quietly worsening performance problem that's easy to miss until a table has been accumulating history for a year or two.

It's worth explicitly recognizing why this "recent data only" pattern deserves special attention as tables grow over the life of a real system: a report that scans the whole table might perform acceptably when the table has 50,000 rows, mediocre when it grows to 400,000, and unacceptably slow once it reaches several million — even though the actual amount of data the report cares about (one recent month) stays roughly constant the entire time. This is a classic "boiling frog" performance problem: nothing dramatic happens at any single point, the report just quietly gets a little slower every month as more history piles up behind it, until one day it's noticeably, painfully slow and nobody remembers exactly when it started. Building the right index — one that seeks the recent range and covers the aggregate's columns — turns this into a report whose performance stays flat over time, regardless of how much historical data accumulates, which is exactly the kind of fix worth making proactively on any report you know is meant to focus on "the recent slice" of an ever-growing table.

One more thing worth knowing: because this index is built around 'recent data,' it stays useful indefinitely even as the table grows to hold years of history, since the report always seeks to a recent starting point and reads forward only a small, roughly constant amount from there -- the index's total size grows with the whole table, but the actual work done per report execution does not.

## Scenario
A month-end summary totals payments by method for December: `SELECT Method, SUM(Amount) ... WHERE PaidAt >= '2025-12-01' GROUP BY Method`. December is ~1/12 of the data, but the report reads all 400,000 rows every time.

## Why it's slow
There's no index on `PaidAt`, so the only way to find December's rows is a **Clustered Index Scan** of the whole table; the date filter is applied afterward. The aggregation itself is cheap — the cost is reading every row to locate the recent slice.

## What to look for
- A Clustered Index Scan feeding the aggregate, with reads across the full table.
- Only a fraction of the scanned rows actually qualify for the date range.

## The concept
Give the range predicate an index and let it **cover** the aggregate: `(PaidAt)` as the key, with `Method` and `Amount` as `INCLUDE`d columns. Now the engine range-seeks straight to December and reads only those rows and only the columns the query needs — no scan, no trip to the base table. (The grouping still uses a hash aggregate, but over a small slice instead of the whole table.)
startingQuery:
SELECT Method, SUM(Amount) AS Total
FROM Payments
WHERE PaidAt >= '2025-12-01'
GROUP BY Method;
hints: The date filter has no index, so the whole table is scanned before the range is applied.
An index on PaidAt would let the query seek straight to December; INCLUDE the columns it aggregates so no lookup is needed.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Payments_PaidAt ON Payments(PaidAt) INCLUDE (Method, Amount);
